Tim Wallace is the Telegraph's Deputy Economics Editor. He has reported on business, finance and the economy since 2010 and joined the Telegraph in 2015. He has won the Economic Research Council’s annual forecasting competition.

British workers face “very, very painful” job losses as AI sweeps through the economy, the chairman of the Office for Budget Responsibility has warned.

Jonathan Haskel said workers should brace for “bad things” as the emerging technology automates more roles .

Mr Haskel said: “AI will displace some people’s jobs, let’s make no bones about that. It’ll be incredibly helpful to other people, on the other hand, and it’s also the case that in all the industrial revolutions we’ve seen thus far, new jobs have been invented and new tasks have come along.

“That can be a very, very painful process, and the idea that it can happen without bad things happening is obviously completely wrong, and we would want people to be helped during that very painful process.”

The comments, made on an Institute for Fiscal Studies podcast, are the starkest warning yet from Britain’s spending watchdog about the negative effects of AI.

Mr Haskel, who previously served on the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, described himself as a “techno-optimist” and said AI should boost productivity in the economy.

He added: “The first thing is it’s going to improve the productivity of the very innovation process itself. We’re going to invent better medicines and better ways of doing things.

“And the second thing is those improvements are then going to spread out in the economy.”

But those who lose out from the process will need help getting into new jobs, he said, to “make a good transition” to the world of AI.

His comments came after investment in AI was shown to have boosted economic growth , helping GDP expand by 0.7pc in the third quarter of the year.

The Bank of England estimates that around one-fifth of this year’s growth has come from AI spending.

However, the effect on workers’ output has been more limited, and it is expected to take time before businesses and their staff find ways to put the new technology to effective use to improve productivity and living standards.

The rise of the technology has also been blamed for reducing hiring in the economy, as businesses spend money on AI and wait to see which staff they may need in future.

### Vacancies at lowest level since Covid

Fewer than 700,000 job vacancies are currently available, according to the Office for National Statistics.

That is the lowest number since the depths of the Covid lockdowns and a figure not seen outside the pandemic since 2014, when the jobs market was still recovering from the financial crisis.

The number of people moving from one job to another has also slumped back to below pre-Covid levels in the past two years, while the situation among young people is at crisis point .

Almost a million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in employment, education or training.

Alan Milburn is set to publish his review of young people and work next week, with recommendations expected to include a reduction in certain benefit payments and an increase in spending on employment support.
